newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Nov 21.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Nov 21.

text.p: THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

US President Bill Clinton yesterday detailed a three-part policy plan centred around liberalisation, democratisation and security, for the purpose of strengthening US-Asia relations. In his speech to the Australian Parliament in Canberra, Clinton rejected any plan of containment for China and vowed to make it a genuine partner. Page 1.

Asia-Pacific countries have rejected plans for free trade in primary energy products by the year 2000 - an initiative Australia was to put to this year's APEC summit. The US and China also appear to be brushing aside Australia's business visa proposal. The collapse of the two initiatives proves an embarrassing problem for Australia as it tries to strengthen its ties with Asia. Page 2.

At a meeting originally scheduled to last 30 minutes, US First Lady Hillary Clinton and Health Minister Michael Wooldridge discussed reform of the Australian and United States health systems in a one-hour private meeting yesterday. Clinton was particulary interested in the issue of keeping health costs from ballooning out of control, with the US experiencing rates of increase about double Australia's six per cent a year increase since the introduction of Medicare in 1983. Page 4.

The World Trade Organisation has lashed out at the US for its attempt to use the Section 301 legislation to impose sanctions on the textile and car industry in other countries. WTO has criticised the US for using channels outside the normal multilateral sstem. The attack came as a deal between Australia and the US was being negotiated which would remove any threat by the US of using the legislation against an Australian leather producer. Page 4.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Addressing a joint-sitting of Federal Parliament yesterday, US President Bill Clinton said the United States was committed to working with Australia to break down the barriers that still restrain global trade and creating an Asia-Pacific community of "shared destiny". Before the address, Clinton laid a wreath at the Australian War Memorial, attended a lunch with more than 600 guests and held two hours of talks with Prime Minister John Howard and his senior Ministers. Page 1.

The Hobart Supreme Court heard yesterday that Martin Bryant was intellectually impaired but not crriminally insane when he murdered 35 people at Port Arthur. Bryant's counsel, John Avery, said Bryant had expected to die during the massacre, but was now resigned to spending the rest of his life in jail.
Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard has approved health insurance premium increases of up to 15 percent, covering over three million people, for Australia's two largest health funds, Medibank Private and MBF. Medibank Private said yesterday it would raise insurance premiums by an average of 12.9 percent, effective December 9, and MBF will increase the cost of its top hospital cover by up to 15 percent from next February. Page 1.

Australia's biggest Internet service provider, OzEmail, announced yesterday it would make cheaper long-distance fax calls available to anyone with an ordinary facsimile machine and telephone connection from December 15, claiming its Internet technology wold make long-distance faxes to selected countries half the price of any sent via Telstra's ordinary telephone network. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Visiting US President Bill Clinton foreshadowed a breakthrough in the long-running dispute over Australian assistance to manufacturing exporters yesterday and also promised Prime Minister John Howard that Australian farmers would be protected in the battle between the United States and Europe over agricultural subsidies. Page 1.

After giving an address on women in the 21st century, US First Lady Hillary Clinton will meet with about 30 Australian women today. The guest list for the function has sparked some controversy, with several notable names excluded from the list, including Democrats Leader Cheryl Kernot, ACTU president Jennie George and the New South Wales Government's three women Ministers. Page 1.

Former stripper and prostitute Kim Hollingsworth's case for unfair dismissal from the New South Wales police force went before the Industrial Relations Commission this week, where she is claiming she was dismissed from the force only two months after she began her training because she worked undercover for the Police Royal Commission to expose corruption within the force. Page 1.

The Carr Cabinet suffered its first loss at the hands of the New South Wales Caucus yesterday, when it voted against a plan to deny sacked police officers the right of appeal. Concerned that Police Commissioner Peter Ryan's plan to allow officers to appeal only to the Supreme Court would set a precedent for other workers, the Caucus voted to permit police to take unfair dismissal cases to the Industrial Relations Commission. Page 1.
THE AGE

In an historic address to both houses of Australian Parliament yesterday, US President Bill Clinton vowed to strengthen his nation's involvement with Asia, as well as to allay concerns about US military presence in China. Clinton said the direction China took in the years ahead would determine whether the next century would be one of conflict or cooperation. Page A1.

Victorian Auditor-general Ches Baragwanath has accused the Kennett Government of breaching the founding principles of the Westminster system in its attempt to allow Government agencies to appoint their own auditors. Baragwanath said the move could seriousy compromise his freedom to independently audit the Government on behalf of the taxpayers. Page A1.

Parents' groups, students and teachers will join forces today in protest against threats from Federal and State funding cuts to public education. While some classes will go ahead as scheduled, some exams for the senior classes will be disrupted. Protesters will march to State Parliament with some teachers expected to condemn pressure to close 113 schools. Page A3.

The Victorian Opposition has branded State solicitor-general Douglas Graham as unfit for his position. The attack in State Parliament yesterday saw criticism directed at Graham for his decision not to prosecute BHP for contempt of court earlier this year because of his A$1 million share interest in the company. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
